title: 2  Chapter 1: Reading and Writing an APA Style Paper
text:
Reading an APA paper can seem like a daunting task at first glance. Some articles can be dozens of pages and the results section can make the statistically-weak-stomached run and hide!
The key to reading an APA paper is to break it down into its sections

2.0.0.1 Abstract


2.0.0.2 Introduction/Background


2.0.0.3 Method


2.0.0.4 Results


2.0.0.5 Discussion


2.0.0.6 References

title: 3  Chapter 2: Working with Descriptive Statistics
text:
Descriptive statistics describe what the data looks like. You likely recall seeing the bell curve in PSY248 (statistics). You may even remember the phrase central tendency. The idea behind these values is that they give us a metric of where the data (likely) comes from.
Let’s go over the usual suspects: Mean, Median, Mode, and Range

3.0.0.1 Mean
The mean represents the average of a set of numbers. Mathematically represented by the following equation:
\(\overline{X}=\frac{\Sigma x}{n}\)
In a simple group, the mean can be seen by eyeballing the data:

x <- rnorm(5,1,0)
x

[1] 1 1 1 1 1


The only number that exists here is 1, so the mean has to be 1…right?!

paste0("The mean of x = ", mean(x))

[1] "The mean of x = 1"


However, when the numbers become more spread out and varied, it is not as easy.

y <- rnorm(15,5,2) |> round(0)
y

 [1] 8 5 4 4 6 3 5 8 4 4 7 7 4 4 3


Eyeballing this data will not do us any good!

paste0("The mean of y = ", mean(y) |> round(2))

[1] "The mean of y = 5.07"


\(\sigma = \frac{\Sigma (x- \overline{x} }{n-1}\)






Never trust the eyeballing of data as a replacement for calculation!








3.0.0.2 Test

text: Dave Brocker

text: Dave Brocker

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Pause and Discuss

How do you know if a study really supports what people say about it?

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Variables vs. Constants









Aspect
Variable
Constant




Example
Age of participants (18, 25, 40…)
All participants are 25 years old


Example
Type of therapy (CBT, DBT, psychoanalysis)
All participants receive CBT only


Example
Reaction time on a cognitive task
All participants finish in exactly 30 seconds


Example
Classroom temperature (varies by room)
Temperature held at 72°F in every room


Example
Number of siblings (0, 1, 2…)
All participants are only children


Role in research
Helps identify relationships, effects, or trends
Used to control conditions / ensure uniformity


Measured or manipulated?
Yes — either, depending on study design
No — typically held constant to reduce confounding

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Measured and Manipulated Variables
A measured variable is recorded as it naturally occurs. A manipulated variable is one the researcher controls — assigning participants to specific levels.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Pause and Discuss

How Would You Classify These Variables?

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
section: From Conceptual Variables to Operational Definitions
text:
From Conceptual Variables to Operational Definitions

Five Real Examples









Variable
Operational Definition
Levels
Measured or Manipulated?




Car ownership
Circled “I own a car” / “I do not own a car”
2 levels
Measured


Expressing gratitude to a partner
Agreement with items like “I tell my partner often that s/he is the best”
7 levels (1–7)
Measured


Exposure to disinformation
Heard false information once or twice
2 levels
Manipulated


Disgust Sensitivity
Score 0–4, higher = more disgusted
Continuous
Measured


Level of anxiety
Heart-rate monitor; >2 SD above baseline BPM = high anxiety
Continuous
Measured









TipAn operational definition turns a vague concept into something you can actually measure or manipulate.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Pause and Discuss

How Would You Operationalize “School Achievement”?

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Three Claims
Every research claim falls into one of three types: Frequency, Association, or Causal.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Frequency Claims

“60% of college students report feeling stressed during finals week.”
A frequency claim describes how often something occurs in a population — no comparison, no relationship, just a rate.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Association Claims
A frequency claim about two variables at once — how they move together.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Positive Association
Amount of weekly exercise ↔︎ Income
Less exercise → lower income. More exercise → higher income. (Both go the same direction.)

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Negative Association
Amount of coffee consumption ↔︎ Degree of depression
Less coffee → lower depression. More coffee → higher depression. (They move in opposite directions.)






ImportantAn association is not a cause



Knowing two variables move together tells you nothing yet about whether one causes the other — that’s the whole reason Causal Claims get their own, stricter set of rules.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Zero Association
Time of dinner ↔︎ a second variable that doesn’t reliably move with it — no consistent pattern either direction.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Making Predictions Based on Associations
Once you know two variables are associated, you can predict one from the other — but prediction is not the same as causal control.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Causal Claims
A causal claim says one variable produces a change in another — the strongest, and hardest to earn, of the three claim types.






ImportantCausal claims need three things



Covariance, temporal precedence, and internal validity (ruling out other explanations) — each gets its own deep dive in the Four Validities lecture.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
A Claim You’ve Probably Seen

The “Kubrick Stare”

A Clockwork Orange, The Shining, Wednesday — internet claims that this camera angle (chin down, eyes up) reliably signals “this character is unhinged.” Is that a real pattern, or pattern-matching after the fact?

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
section: Not All Claims Are Based on Research
text:
Not All Claims Are Based on Research


“You just need folic acid, B complex — this stuff makes your pee bright yellow — and magnesium. Combine those three with a bit of water and — chef’s kiss — no hangover! Coming from the queen of hangovers, try it.”







TipThe whole point of this course



Learning to tell the difference between a claim like this one and a claim backed by actual research.

title: Three Claims: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Key Takeaways

Three Claims

Variables vary; constants don’t — and operational definitions turn vague concepts into something measurable
Every research claim is a Frequency, Association, or Causal claim
Associations can be positive, negative, or zero — but none of them, by themselves, prove causation
Causal claims carry the highest bar: covariance, temporal precedence, and internal validity, all three

text:
Dave Brocker — PSY 360, Lab 3







TipTwo skills, one lab



Formatting references correctly and writing a testable hypothesis are separate skills, but both are about being precise — precise about where an idea came from, and precise about what you’re predicting.

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
text:
APA Style, 7th Edition

Reference-list and in-text citation formatting follows the APA 7th edition manual.






ImportantWhere to look this up




Purdue OWL’s APA guide is a reliable, free reference for exact formatting of journal articles, books, and websites.

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
section: What Are the Characteristics of a Good Hypothesis?
text:
What Are the Characteristics of a Good Hypothesis?

Logical
The logical conclusion of a logical argument


Testable
All of the variables, events, and individuals can be defined and observed


Refutable
Can be demonstrated to be false


Positive
Must make a positive statement about the existence of something

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
text:
Refutable: “Falsifiable”
A hypothesis is refutable (or “falsifiable”) when it’s possible for the outcome to be different from the prediction — there has to be some result that would prove it wrong.

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
text:
BAD Hypothesis!


“The human mind emits thought waves that influence other people, but that cannot be measured or recorded in any way.”







ImportantWhy this fails



If it can’t be measured or recorded in any way, there’s no possible result that could disprove it. Not refutable — not a testable hypothesis.

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
text:
Positive: A Real Example

A hypothesis has to claim that something does exist or does happen — not just that something doesn’t.

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
text:
Examples of Good Hypotheses

For high school students, there is a relationship between intelligence and creativity.

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
text:
Examples of Good Hypotheses

There is a difference between the verbal skills of 3-year-old girls and those of 3-year-old boys.

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
text:
Examples of Good Hypotheses

The new therapy technique will produce significant improvement for severely depressed patients.






TipWhat makes these work



Each one names specific variables, is stated as a positive claim, and could turn out to be false — the three things a testable hypothesis needs.

title: APA Style Reference Formatting and Writing a Hypothesis
text:
Final Topic and Annotated Bibliography

All assignments should be submitted electronically on Brightspace.

Individual work, shared sources
Each member needs to submit their own assignment, in their own words. Group members may annotate the same reference — but consider finding and summarizing independent sources and sharing with one another.

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text: Dave Brocker Lecturer Farmingdale State College

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text: Dave Brocker Lecturer Farmingdale State College

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Why This Matters

A Skill You’ll Use All Semester
Reading an APA-style paper can seem daunting — some articles run a dozen pages, and the Results section can send the statistically faint of heart running for the hills!
The fix isn’t reading faster. It’s reading the paper in the order it was built to be read, section by section.

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
section: The Six Sections of an APA Paper
text:
The Six Sections of an APA Paper

Abstract
One paragraph, the whole study


Introduction / Background
Why this study? What’s already known?


Method
Who, what, and how


Results
What did the data show?


Discussion
What does it mean?


References
Where the claims come from

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Abstract

One Paragraph, the Whole Study
The abstract is a 150–250 word summary that previews every other section: the question, the method, the key result, and why it matters.






TipRead the abstract first, always



It tells you whether the rest of the paper is worth your time — and what to expect from each section that follows.

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Introduction / Background

Why This Study? What’s Already Known?
The introduction builds the case for the study, moving from broad context to the specific question:

What do we already know, based on prior research?
What’s the gap, disagreement, or open question?
What does this study specifically test, and what’s the hypothesis?

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Method

Who, What, and How
The Method section is the recipe — detailed enough that another researcher could run the same study again.

Participants: who was studied, and how were they recruited?
Materials/Measures: what instruments, surveys, or apparatus were used?
Procedure: what did participants actually do, in order?

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Results

What Did the Data Show?
Results reports what was found, without yet interpreting what it means.

Descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations)
The statistical test(s) used, and whether the result was significant
Tables and figures that summarize the pattern in the data







ImportantResults describes; it doesn’t explain



Save the “why” and “so what” for the Discussion section — mixing the two is a common early-writer mistake.

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Discussion

What Does It Mean?
The discussion interprets the results in light of the original question:

Did the data support the hypothesis?
How does this fit with (or challenge) prior research from the Introduction?
What are the limitations, and what should future research look at?

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
References

Where the Claims Come From
Every claim in the Introduction and Discussion should trace back to a source listed here, in APA citation format. This is also your best tool for finding more papers.

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Pause and Discuss

Finding Related Work
Pick one article from your literature search. If you clicked “Cited By” on it, what showed up — newer studies that built on it, or studies that argued against it?

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Check Your Understanding


You only have time to skim one paper before lab. Which section do you read first, and why?

The Abstract — it’s built to answer exactly that question in under a minute, and tells you whether the full paper is worth a closer read.



A paper’s Results section reports a result, but never says what it means for the field. Is that a problem?

No — that’s expected. Interpretation belongs in the Discussion section, not Results.

title: Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper
text:
Key Takeaways

Reading and Writing an APA-Style Paper

APA papers follow a fixed structure for a reason: it lets you read strategically instead of front-to-back
Abstract → Introduction → Method → Results → Discussion → References, each with its own job
You’ll draft each of these sections yourself this semester, one lab at a time

title: Lab 1: Brainstorming Research Ideas
text:

How Do You Choose?

title: Lab 1: Brainstorming Research Ideas
text:
Operationalization

But What Does It All Mean?
What do you mean, “social media use changes mood”?


How they score on a mood questionnaire?

One valid operationalization — a self-report measure.



How they behave toward others in social situations?

A behavioral measure — observed interaction, not self-report.



How easily they become frustrated?

A different behavioral proxy — reaction to a frustrating task.



How their facial expressions change?

A physiological/expressive measure — could be coded from video.



How they interpret an ambiguous scene?

A cognitive/interpretive measure — often used in mood-congruent judgment studies.

Key Takeaways

Brainstorming Research Ideas

A good topic starts anywhere — movies, personal experience, the news — but has to hold up to IRB scrutiny: minimal risk, benign, no deception, anonymous

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Dave Brocker







TipOnce you’ve identified the kind of claim, you need to be able to evaluate it.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Dave Brocker







TipOnce you’ve identified the kind of claim, you need to be able to evaluate it.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
The Four Big Validities


Construct Validity
Does the measure or manipulation really capture the thing it claims to?


External Validity
Does the result generalize beyond this sample and setting?


Statistical Validity
How precise and reliable is the statistical estimate?


Internal Validity
For causal claims — have other explanations been ruled out?

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Interrogating Frequency Claims

“74% of the world smiled yesterday.”

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Construct Validity
Does “smiled yesterday” actually capture happiness — or just a momentary facial expression, possibly to a stranger with a clipboard?

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
External Validity
Does the sample who answered this survey represent “the world,” or just the people who happened to be reachable?

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Statistical Validity

Point Estimate, Confidence Interval, Margin of Error
A point estimate (like “74%”) is a single best guess. A confidence interval gives the plausible range around it.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Confidence Interval: Example
39% point estimate, 95% CI: 37.0% – 41.4%






TipMargin of error



Half the width of the confidence interval — a smaller margin means a more precise (more statistically valid) estimate.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Interrogating Association Claims

Coffee Consumption ↔︎ Depression

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Construct Validity

Two Constructs, Two Checks
For an association claim, you check construct validity twice — once for each variable.

Coffee Consumption
Self-reported cups per day? A tracked purchase log? Each captures something slightly different.


Depression

A validated clinical scale? A single self-rating question? The construct validity of this measure shapes how much the association claim is worth.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
External Validity
Does this coffee/depression relationship hold for people outside the sample it was studied in — different ages, cultures, caffeine tolerances?

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Statistical Validity
Same tools as before — how precise is the estimate of how strongly these two variables are associated?

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Interrogating Causal Claims

The Hardest Bar to Clear

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Covariance
A and B have to actually move together — if they don’t covary, there’s no relationship to explain causally in the first place.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Temporal Precedence
A has to come before B — not the other way around, and not at the same time in a way that makes order unclear.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Internal Validity

Rule out C — some third variable that could explain the A–B relationship without A actually causing B.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Experiments Can Support Causal Claims
Because a well-designed experiment can establish all three: the researcher creates covariance (by manipulating the IV), controls temporal precedence (IV comes first, DV is measured after), and rules out confounds (random assignment spreads other differences evenly across groups).

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Independent and Dependent Variables

The independent variable (IV) is what the researcher manipulates (e.g., type of lessons). The dependent variable (DV) is what gets measured as a result.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Random Assignment
Assigning participants to conditions by chance — the mechanism that makes “rule out other explanations” actually work, by spreading pre-existing differences evenly across groups.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
section: When Causal Claims Are a Mistake
text:
When Causal Claims Are a Mistake

Does Social Media Pressure Cause Teen Anxiety?

A real headline claim — but does it actually meet the three criteria?

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
section: Does It Meet the Three Criteria?
text:
Does It Meet the Three Criteria?

Covariance?
Plausible — more social media use tends to co-occur with more anxiety.


Temporal Precedence?
Harder to establish — does the pressure to respond to texts and posts come before the anxiety, or does anxiety drive more checking?


Internal Validity?
Third variables (sleep, existing mental health, family circumstances) haven’t been ruled out in most of these studies.







ImportantCovariance alone is not enough



This is exactly the pattern that turns a real association into an overreaching causal headline.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
section: Other Validities to Interrogate in Causal Claims
text:
Other Validities to Interrogate in Causal Claims
Even once covariance, temporal precedence, and internal validity are addressed, the same Construct, External, and Statistical validity questions from frequency and association claims still apply — a causal claim can fail on any of the four.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Prioritizing Validities

Not every validity matters equally for every claim. For a causal claim, internal validity usually matters most. For a claim about how common something is, statistical and external validity carry more weight.

title: Four Validities: Interrogation Tools for Consumers of Research
text:
Key Takeaways

Four Validities

Every claim — frequency, association, or causal — can be interrogated with the same four validities: Construct, External, Statistical, Internal
Construct validity asks whether you’re really measuring what you think you’re measuring
Causal claims carry a stricter bar: covariance, temporal precedence, and ruling out third variables
Well-designed experiments (manipulated IV, random assignment) are what let you clear that bar

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text: Dave Brocker

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text: Dave Brocker

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Ways to Measure Variables

Any variable can be expressed in two ways: a conceptual definition (the abstract idea) and an operational definition (exactly how it’s measured).

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
How Can We Operationalize “Happiness”?


Conceptual Definition of “Happiness”
A subjective sense of well-being and life satisfaction


Operational Definition of “Happiness”
e.g., a 7-point self-report scale, or the frequency of smiling observed over an hour

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Operationalizing Other Conceptual Variables
Every abstract construct in a study — stress, motivation, aggression — needs an operational definition before it can actually be measured.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Three Common Types of Measures


Self-Report
Asking people to describe themselves


Observation
Watching and coding behavior


Physiological
Recording a bodily response

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Self-Report Measures: Caffeine Consumption

e.g., asking someone how many cups of coffee they drink per day.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Observational (Behavioral) Measures

How could you operationalize allergies, or cleanliness, by observing behavior rather than asking?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text: Physiological Measures

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Scales of Measurement

Categorical Variables
Groups with no inherent order


Quantitative Variables
Values that can be ordered or measured on a continuum

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Categorical Variables (Nominal)

Species — Rhesus Monkey, Bonobo, Chimpanzee — is a nominal variable: categories with no meaningful order or distance between them.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Types of Quantitative Variables

Ordinal Scale
Ranked order, but unequal spacing


Interval Scale
Equal spacing, but no true zero


Ratio Scale
Equal spacing and a true zero

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Ordinal Scale: Ranked Order

Coffee sizes — Short (8 fl oz), Tall, Grande, Venti — are ranked in order, but the size difference between each step isn’t consistent from one chain to the next.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Interval Scale

Equal intervals between points, but 0 doesn’t mean “nothing.” (Think of a temperature scale — 0°F isn’t the absence of temperature.)

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Ratio Scale

Equal intervals and a true zero that means “none of the thing exists” — which makes ratio statements meaningful (twice as much, half as much).

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Selecting a Scale of Measurement

Nominal
Categories only — no order


Ordinal
Ranked, unequal spacing


Interval
Equal spacing, no true zero


Ratio
Equal spacing, true zero

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Reliability

Test-Retest Reliability
Consistency across time


Interrater Reliability
Consistency across raters


Internal Reliability
Consistency across items

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Test-Retest Reliability

Do people get consistent scores if the same measure is given at Time 1, Time 2, and Time 3?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Interrater Reliability

Do two independent raters, coding the same event, arrive at consistent ratings?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Internal Reliability (Internal Consistency)
Do people give consistent responses across every item on the same questionnaire — i.e., do the items “hang together”?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Evaluating Reliability with a Scatterplot

Higher interrater reliability shows up as dots clustered close to the diagonal line; lower reliability shows up as dots spread further from it.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Using the Correlation Coefficient r

Although a scatterplot is a good first step, the more common and efficient way to evaluate reliability is the correlation coefficient, ranging from -1 to +1.






TipStrength



The tighter the spread of dots in a scatterplot, the stronger the correlation — and the higher the reliability.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Test-Retest Reliability: Reading the Number

Good Test-Retest Reliability
r is strong and positive — .5 or above


Low Test-Retest Reliability
r is positive but weak

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Interrater Reliability: Reading the Number

Good Interrater Reliability
r is positive and strong — .7 or higher


Terrible Interrater Reliability
r is negative

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Internal Reliability: Average Inter-Item Correlation
Internal reliability is typically evaluated with the average inter-item correlation — how consistently each item on a scale correlates with every other item.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
section: Reading About Reliability in Journal Articles
text:
Reading About Reliability in Journal Articles

When a published study reports “Cronbach’s α = .85” or “test-retest r = .72,” that’s the same logic covered here — just applied and reported in a real paper.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability
text:
Key Takeaways

Identifying Good Measurement: Reliability

Every variable needs both a conceptual definition (the idea) and an operational definition (exactly how it’s measured)
Scales of measurement — nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio — determine what kinds of comparisons are meaningful
Three reliability types: test-retest (across time), interrater (across raters), internal (across items)
The correlation coefficient r is the standard tool for evaluating reliability — closer to ±1 means a stronger, more reliable relationship

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Dave Brocker







TipThe core question



Once you’ve operationalized a variable, how do you know your measure actually captures what you intended it to?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Dave Brocker







TipThe core question



Once you’ve operationalized a variable, how do you know your measure actually captures what you intended it to?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Operationalizing Disgust
How could you measure — operationalize — disgust?






ImportantThere’s no single right answer



A facial-expression code, a self-report scale, a physiological measure (skin conductance) — each operationalization captures disgust a little differently, and each has to be validated on its own.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Operationalizing Depression
How could you measure — operationalize — depression?
Same challenge: a clinical interview, a self-report inventory (like the BDI), or a diagnostic code from a medical record are all different operationalizations of the same abstract construct.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Subjective Ways to Assess Validity

Face Validity
It looks like what you want to measure


Content Validity
The measure contains all the parts that your theory says it should contain

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Empirical Ways to Assess Validity

Criterion Validity
Your measure is correlated with a relevant behavioral outcome


Convergent Validity
Your self-report measure is more strongly associated with self-report measures of similar constructs


Discriminant Validity
Your self-report measure is less strongly associated with self-report measures of dissimilar constructs

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Empirical Ways to Assess Reliability

Test-Retest
People get consistent scores every time they take the test


Internal Reliability
People give consistent responses on every item of a questionnaire


Interrater Reliability
Two coders’ ratings of a set of targets are consistent with each other

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Measurement Validity of Abstract Constructs

Abstract constructs (happiness, disgust, depression) can’t be measured directly — every validity check below is about how confident you can be that an indirect measure is actually tracking the construct.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
section: Does It Correlate with Key Behaviors?
text: Does It Correlate with Key Behaviors?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Criterion Validity
Does your measure correlate with a relevant, real-world behavioral outcome?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Known-Groups Evidence for Criterion Validity

One way to test criterion validity: does the measure distinguish between groups who are already known to differ on the construct?

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Known-Groups: A Real Example
Psychiatrists’ independent categorizations of patients are compared against scores on the measure being validated — if the groups a psychiatrist would identify score differently, that’s evidence the measure is tracking something real.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Known-Groups Evidence for Criterion Validity

Which groups have the highest and lowest subjective well-being (SWB) scores? If the pattern matches what theory predicts, that’s supporting evidence for criterion validity.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Convergent Validity

r = .68 between the CES-D (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale) and the BDI (Beck Depression Inventory) — two different measures of the same construct (depression), strongly correlated.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Discriminant (Divergent) Validity

r = .16 between the BDI (a depression measure) and a Physical Health Measure — a different construct, weakly correlated, as it should be.






TipWhy both matter



Convergent validity shows your measure relates strongly to things it should relate to. Discriminant validity shows it doesn’t relate too strongly to things it shouldn’t — together they’re stronger evidence than either alone.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
section: The Relationship Between Reliability and Validity
text:
The Relationship Between Reliability and Validity


Reliable, Not Valid
Consistent, but consistently off-target


Valid, Not Reliable
On-target on average, but scattered


Neither Reliable Nor Valid
Scattered and off-target


Both Reliable and Valid
Consistent and on-target







ImportantReliability is a prerequisite for validity



A measure has to give consistent results before it’s even possible to ask whether it’s measuring the right thing. Reliable does not guarantee valid — but unreliable guarantees not valid.

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text: Reliability Exercise

title: Identifying Good Measurement: Validity
text:
Key Takeaways

Identifying Good Measurement: Validity

Subjective checks (face, content validity) and empirical checks (criterion, convergent, discriminant) both matter — but empirical checks carry more weight
Known-groups evidence and criterion validity ask whether a measure behaves the way theory predicts it should
Convergent validity (strong correlation with similar measures) and discriminant validity (weak correlation with dissimilar measures) work together
Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity — a measure must be consistent before it can be evaluated as accurate

Dave Brocker







TipThe opening question



Should psychologists use deception or attempt to produce certain feelings in their research participants?

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Ethical Guidelines
for Research Psychology

Dave Brocker







The opening question


Should psychologists use deception or attempt to produce certain feelings in their research participants?

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Example: Kassin et al. (1996)

A study on false confessions — participants were accused of a crash they didn’t cause (pressing the ALT key) after their computer “crashed.”

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Experimental Design

Participants
79 undergraduates — 40 male, 39 female


IV 1: Vulnerability
High vs. Low Vulnerability


IV 2: Witness
Witness vs. No Witness

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
The Method
Participants were told not to press the ALT key. 60 seconds later, the computer crashed — and a confederate suggested the participant had caused it by pressing the forbidden key.






The ethical tension


No participant actually caused the crash. The study measured whether people would falsely confess — which meant deceiving every participant about what really happened.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
What Is Research Ethics?
Guided by the American Psychological Association’s ethical principles for research.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Historical Highlights
Treatment of Human Participants in Research
The modern rules governing research ethics didn’t come from nowhere — they came from real cases where researchers caused real harm.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
The Nuremberg Trials

The prosecution of Nazi physicians for experiments conducted on concentration camp prisoners without consent led to the Nuremberg Code (1947) — the first major international standard for research ethics.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
The Tuskegee Study (1932–1972)

Researchers withheld treatment from Black men with syphilis for 40 years — even after penicillin became a known, effective cure — without informing participants of their diagnosis or the existence of treatment.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Milgram (1963): Obedience to Authority

Participants were instructed to administer what they believed were increasingly severe electric shocks to another person, testing how far people would go under the instruction of an authority figure.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
section: Zimbardo & Haney (1971): The Stanford Prison Experiment
text:
Zimbardo & Haney (1971): The Stanford Prison Experiment

Participants randomly assigned to “guard” and “prisoner” roles in a simulated prison — ended early after guards began behaving abusively toward prisoners.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
A Modern Example: Abu Ghraib

The dynamics observed in the Stanford Prison Experiment have been cited as a lens for understanding real abuses of institutional power decades later.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
From History to Policy


U.S. Surgeon General (late 1960s)
First federal guidelines requiring informed consent for federally funded research


National Research Act (1974)
Established Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) in law


Belmont Report (1979)
The ethical framework still used today

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
The Belmont Report (1979)

Three core principles for ethical research with human subjects:

Respect for Persons
Treat people as autonomous agents; extra protections for those with diminished autonomy


Beneficence
Maximize possible benefits, minimize possible harms


Justice
Fairness in who bears the burdens and who receives the benefits of research

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
APA Ethics Code
Updated and expanded many times, periodically reviewed. Ten standards total — Section 8: Research and Publication is the one most relevant to conducting a study.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Major Ethical Issues

Clinical Equipoise
Subjects must be protected from physical or psychological harm.


Informed Consent
Participants must understand what they’re agreeing to before they agree to it.


Deception
When is it justified, and what has to happen afterward?


Confidentiality
Protecting what participants share.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
section: Selected Components of an Informed Consent Form
text:
Selected Components of an Informed Consent Form

A real consent form typically covers: the purpose of the study, what participation involves, risks and benefits, confidentiality protections, and the right to withdraw at any time without penalty.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Deception

Everyday example
“Everything works great on this car!” (Lie — don’t mention what doesn’t work)


Everyday example
“I can totally speak 3 different languages!” (Lie — applies for a bilingual position)

Research deception works the same way: withholding or misrepresenting the true purpose of a study from participants.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Deception: Guidelines

Deception is only permissible when there’s no reasonable non-deceptive alternative, no expectation of serious harm, and participants are debriefed afterward.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Confidentiality
Protecting participants’ data and identities — from the raw data itself through to how results are reported and published.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
The Institutional Review Board (IRB)

Every institution conducting research with human subjects has an IRB that reviews proposed studies before they begin, weighing the risks to participants against the study’s scientific value.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
section: Is It Ethical to Use Animals in Behavioral Research?
text:
Is It Ethical to Use Animals in Behavioral Research?
Why do researchers use nonhuman subjects at all? Some questions can’t ethically (or practically) be studied in humans — but that doesn’t remove the ethical obligations toward the animals involved.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Protections for Animal Subjects

Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUCs) play a role analogous to an IRB — reviewing study design, housing, and treatment of animal subjects.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Ethical Decision Making

A Thoughtful Balance
Ethical research design is rarely a simple checklist — it’s weighing scientific value against risk to participants, case by case.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Ethical Issues and Scientific Integrity
Ethics doesn’t stop once data collection ends — how a study is reported and published raises its own set of ethical questions.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
“Fraud” in Science
Fabricating or falsifying data, or misrepresenting results, undermines the entire scientific record other researchers build on.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Safeguards to Prevent Fraud
Peer review, replication, data-sharing requirements, and institutional research integrity offices all exist to catch and deter fraud — though none of them is foolproof.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Plagiarism






Repeating text verbatim is plagiarism — even with a citation






Original text, Quirin, Kazen, & Kuhl (2009):

Are affective experiences like happiness, sadness, or helplessness always amenable to self-report? Whereas many individuals may be able to describe their affective states or traits relatively accurately, others may provide self reports that deviate from their automatic affective reactions.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Plagiarism: Still a Problem
Changing a few words is still plagiarism, even with a citation:

Are people really in touch with their emotional responses? For example, are feelings like happiness, sadness, or helplessness always available for self-report? Whereas many individuals may be able to describe their feelings relatively accurately, others may provide self reports that deviate from their true reactions (Quirin, Kazen, & Kuhl, 2009).

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Plagiarism: Closer, Still a Problem
Changing most of the wording but keeping the same structure and order of ideas is a step toward paraphrasing — but is still plagiarism, even with a citation:

Is it easy for people to report their feelings? Although some people may be able to give accurate reports, others fail to provide accurate descriptions of how they feel (Quirin, Kazen, & Kuhl, 2009).







The takeaway


Real paraphrasing means processing the idea and re-expressing it in your own structure and words, not swapping synonyms into someone else’s sentence.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Large Language Models






Use Caution!








Large language models raise research-ethics questions of their own: from citing AI-assisted writing honestly to the risk of an LLM inventing a citation that doesn’t exist.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Research Psychology
text:
Key Takeaways
Ethical Guidelines for Research

Modern research ethics rules exist because of real historical harm — Nuremberg, Tuskegee, Milgram, and Stanford Prison all shaped today’s standards
The Belmont Report’s three principles — Respect for Persons, Beneficence, Justice — still anchor the APA Ethics Code and IRB review
Informed consent, limits on deception, and confidentiality protect participants; IRBs and IACUCs review studies before they start
Ethics doesn’t end at data collection — fraud and plagiarism (even “just changing some words”) are ethical violations too

A Word on AI

Permissible, With Attribution
You’re permitted and encouraged to use AI tools like ChatGPT on assignments — with proper attribution, and full responsibility for your submission’s accuracy and quality.

title: PSY 360: Research Methods
text:
A Word on AI

Best Practices

Thoroughly review AI output for relevance, depth, inaccuracies, bias, plagiarism, and copyright issues
Never input another person’s likeness, voice, or private information into an AI tool
Never upload copyright-protected or paywalled content
Cite AI as a reference whenever its output is used, quoted, or paraphrased
